div.p: LLM agents increasingly operate in modular systems, where planning requires coordinating multiple functional components whose actions can causally change downstream states and behaviors. This makes intervention-aware prediction essential: an agent must anticipate not only what is likely to happen next, but what will happen as a consequence of its own actions. We find that purely observational world models can incur irreducible intervention-time error in such systems, even when they accurately model observational trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose CausalCompose, a causal world-model framework that equips modular LLM agents with causal structure for intervention-aware prediction and planning. We theoretically show that causal composition can overcome this intervention gap with sufficient evidence and controlled local error. Experiments across diverse modular agent environments validate these results: incorporating causal structure consistently improves intervention-sensitive reasoning and planning, with particularly clear gains in structured tool-use systems where causal dependencies directly govern action execution. Our results show when causal world models help modular LLM agents: when causal dependencies are identifiable and actionable for planning.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: LLM agents increasingly operate in systems that are modular by design [3,15,17,37]. Rather than interacting with a single monolithic environment, an agent often coordinates multiple functional modules [15,17]. For example, a retail agent must coordinate payment and fulfillment services to complete an order [3,36,37], while a household agent must coordinate navigation and object interaction to accomplish a physical task [29]. Modern agent benchmarks make this modular structure increasingly explicit: APIBank [15] organizes interaction around executable APIs, ToolSandbox [17] evaluates stateful tool use, 𝜏-bench [37] and 𝜏 2 -bench [3] couple language interaction with domain tools and evolving environment state, and ALFWorld [29] requires agents to coordinate distinct functional operations over a shared embodied task. This modular organization enables agents to decompose complex tasks into specialized components, reuse functional capabilities across tasks, and coordinate heterogeneous tools and services within a unified workflow. A modular design therefore provides a scalable and flexible foundation for building agents that operate across increasingly complex environments.

This modularity creates a causal problem. Sequence-based world models learn which states and actions tend to occur together, whereas planning requires predicting what will happen because the agent takes a particular action. This distinction becomes fundamental when modules share latent causes or when several components change together: an observationally predictive dependency need not remain valid after intervention [22,24,28]. For example, an agent may repeatedly observe a payment update followed by a shipment transition and learn this sequence accurately, while still predicting the wrong downstream state when it actively changes the payment module. More generally, model-based RL and language-agent world models are commonly trained to predict future observations or trajectories from recorded experience [8-11, 13, 14, 18, 33, 39]. In modular systems, however, accurate observational prediction alone does not guarantee correct intervention-time prediction.

We first formalize why observational world models can fail at intervention time. Even if a world model perfectly learns the predictive relationships present in observational data, those relationships need not correctly predict the consequences of actively changing one module [22,24]. We characterize this mismatch through unblocked back-door paths [22] and prove that, under nondegenerate confounding, the optimal observational predictor still incurs a strictly positive error gap relative to the correct interventional predictor. Thus, collecting more observational data or fitting the observational distribution more accurately cannot in general eliminate the error: resolving it requires information that distinguishes observation from intervention [22,24]. We further show that this problem becomes more consequential in modular systems, because an incorrect intervention prediction at one module can propagate through subsequent module dependencies, causing prediction reliability to deteriorate as the composition depth increases.

To address this problem, we propose CausalCompose, a causal world model for modular LLM agents. Instead of treating the system as one undifferentiated trajectory, CausalComposepreserves local mechanisms and uses local actions and responses to identify causal dependencies among functional modules. As illustrated in We evaluate these predictions through synthetic causal diagnostics and modular LLM-agent environments [3,15,17,29,37]. The synthetic experiments verify the predicted intervention gap, horizon compounding, and dependence of causal recovery on intervention coverage. Agent experiments further show that incorporating causal structure improves intervention-sensitive reasoning and planning, with the clearest gains in structured tool-use environments [3,15,17,37] where modular dependencies directly govern valid actions and downstream transitions. Across dialogue and narrative settings, the experiments further demonstrate that causal knowledge becomes useful when it is presented in a form that makes the relevant dependency actionable at decision time. Together, these results answer the question posed by our title: causal world models help modular LLM agents when intervention-sensitive dependencies can be identified from available evidence and incorporated into agent planning.
Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We identify a fundamental mismatch between observational world modeling and intervention-time planning in modular LLM agents.

(2) We establish the intervention-time error of observational models, characterize its compounding across modules, and derive conditions under which causal composition overcomes this gap. (3) We propose CausalCompose, which learns causal dependencies from intervention-response evidence and composes local mechanisms for prediction and planning. (4) We validate our theory across synthetic diagnostics and modular agent environments, showing when causal world models improve agent planning.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Federated and causal learning. Federated RL [31] shares policies, value functions, or learned models across decentralized clients, while model-based RL learns dynamics for planning and control [8][9][10][11]14]. Causal discovery methods learn structure from observational data [41], interventions or heterogeneous environments [4,23,24], and distributed data [2,12,19]. Unlike settings where clients represent separate environments, CausalCompose treats clients as functional modules of one coupled system and uses interventionresponse evidence to recover and compose dependencies between their local mechanisms.

Causal and language-agent world models. Causal representation learning and causal world models study how causal structure supports generalization, prediction, and control [20,28,40]. Recent LLM-agent work further explores environment simulation, retrieval, dynamic reasoning, adaptive world models, state tracking, and action-conditioned reasoning [1,6,13,18,33,38,39]. We instead ask when causal dependencies between functional modules improve intervention-time prediction and planning.

Agent benchmarks and modular systems. Interactive benchmarks evaluate agents over tool use, service workflows, embodied environments, web interaction, and device control [3,15,17,26,29,32,36,37]. We use their naturally separable functional components to make cross-module dependencies explicit and evaluate when modeling these dependencies causally improves prediction and planning.

div.head: CausalCompose
div.p: CausalCompose turns distributed interaction traces into an intervention-aware world model for modular LLM agents. Rather than fitting a single global transition model, it preserves local mechanisms and learns the causal interfaces needed to compose them. Given 𝐾 modules with local states 𝑋 𝑘,𝑡 , actions 𝐴 𝑘,𝑡 , and transition mechanisms defined in Equation (3.1), CausalCompose identifies and validates cross-module intervention-response dependencies, then composes them for downstream prediction and action selection.

Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline: extracting local interventionresponse evidence, validating causal interfaces, and composing them for prediction and optional control. Modules exchange only compact interface evidence-including events, responses, direction, and lag-rather than complete trajectories, preserving modularity while capturing cross-module causal propagation.

The rate depends on both intervention exposure and response detectability: causal interfaces cannot be reliably recovered if the relevant intervention is never executed or its downstream response cannot be observed. This directly motivates the intervention-response collection stage in Figure 1.

div.head: Intervention-Aware Causal Composition
div.p: Once the interfaces are validated, CausalCompose composes the local mechanisms through the recovered causal structure. As illustrated in Figure 2(a), a candidate intervention is first evaluated by its local mechanism, and the resulting interface event is propagated only to causally connected modules in 𝐺. Each destination module then combines the incoming event with its local state and mechanism to predict subsequent states and downstream effects.

Rather than fitting a global transition function, CausalCompose recursively composes these local mechanisms along validated causal paths. In the linear setting, this propagation is characterized by the total-effect operator in Equation (3.11), which aggregates the effects transmitted along causal paths between modules. Thus, validated interfaces determine where intervention effects propagate, while local mechanisms determine how those effects transform.

The resulting rollout captures both immediate and downstream consequences of a candidate intervention. Unlike Seq-WM, which predicts from observational trajectories, CausalCompose explicitly propagates interventions through the recovered causal structure.

div.head: Optional Causal Control for Action Selection
div.p: Beyond prediction, CausalCompose can use the composed causal model as a closed-loop controller during action selection. As shown in Figure 2(b), at each step the LLM first proposes a candidate action. CausalCompose then checks its upstream prerequisites using P 𝑘 , predicts its local and downstream consequences through the causal composition in Equation (3.11), and gates the action accordingly. Actions with missing prerequisites or conflicting predicted effects are revised; otherwise, the selected action is executed. Execution closes the loop. After observing the resulting downstream state, CausalCompose compares it with the causal prediction. For predicted state 𝑋 𝑗,𝑡 +1 , the residual 𝑒 𝑗,𝑡 +1 = 𝑋 𝑗,𝑡 +1 -𝑋 𝑗,𝑡 +1 measures the prediction-execution mismatch. The observed state and residual are then fed into the next decision step, updating the evidence available for interface verification and informing the next candidate action. The control loop therefore repeats as propose → check → predict → gate → execute → verify → feedback until the task terminates.

This gives CausalCompose two operational modes: predictiononly, where causal composition does not alter the policy, and control, where causal predictions and execution feedback repeatedly guide subsequent decisions. This distinction separates the value of recovering causal structure from the agent's ability to exploit it online.

div.head: Experiments 5.1 Experimental Setup
div.p: We evaluate whether causal world models improve downstream agent behavior, when these gains persist across environments and seeds, and whether the mechanisms predicted by our theory appear under controlled interventions. Our evaluation combines 𝜏-bench retail and airline [37], ALFWorld [29], ScienceWorld [32], APIBank Stateful [15], stateful tool-use environments [17], and a controlled synthetic SCM. The environments span structured API execution, embodied language interaction, and intervention-controlled causal systems.

Our primary non-causal baseline, Seq-WM, predicts from observational trajectories using ReAct-style world-model prompting [27,33,38]. We additionally compare against local, temporal, transition-graph, correlation-based, annotated, and no-worldmodel variants where available. Discovered-Causal uses recovered causal dependencies, while Oracle-Causal receives groundtruth causal structure and serves as a structural reference rather than an empirical upper bound on task success. Our complete method is CausalCompose. Specifically: • Seq-WM [27,33,38]: uses observational trajectories without explicit causal structure. • Local [35]: restricts prediction to locally relevant information.

• Temporal [30]: models dependencies through temporal proximity. • Transition Graph [8,9]: uses observed transition structure without causal semantics. • Correlation-based [22]: uses statistical associations rather than interventional dependencies. • Annotated: provides manually specified task structure or constraints.
• No World Model: removes explicit world-model reasoning.

• Discovered-Causal [40,42]: uses causal dependencies recovered from intervention-response evidence. • Oracle-Causal: uses ground-truth causal structure to isolate structural correctness from discovery error. • CausalCompose: combines causal discovery, validated causal interfaces, and intervention-aware composition.
Unless confidence intervals are reported, agent results should be interpreted as targeted diagnostic comparisons rather than precise benchmark-level rankings.

div.head: When Does Causal Information Help?
div.p: The main results show positive downstream effects, while Table 4 indicates that causal structure is most useful when agents can exploit it during decision making. On 𝜏-bench, highlighting the current goal improves Oracle-Causal from 45% to 75% and Discovered-Causal from 45% to 60% without changing their causal graphs, revealing a strong salience effect [16]. Gains on APIBank Stateful and ScienceWorld, together with positive model effects on 𝜏bench (+4.77 points) and ALFWorld (+8.21 points) and a 10-point gain from immediate feedback, further show that causal information must be accessible, updated, and translated into interventionrelevant actions.

div.head: Efficiency and End-to-End Feasibility
div.p: Finally, we evaluate whether the causal representation improves both performance and execution efficiency. Table 6 shows that CausalCompose improves all three environments with modest or reduced overhead. Retail success increases from 33.33% to 54.86% with one additional call, while ALFWorld improves from 37.31% to 49.55% with slightly fewer calls. On ScienceWorld, the score rises from 14.80 to 17.67 while calls decrease by 42.4%. Thus, causal composition can improve performance without substantial overhead.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented CausalCompose and studied when causal world models help modular LLM agents. Our theory shows that observational errors can persist under intervention and amplify downstream, while causal composition can reduce this gap. Experiments across agent benchmarks and synthetic SCMs support these predictions, with larger benefits under confounding and propagation and smaller gains with informative proxies. We further show that causal structure is most effective when actionable during decision making, while CausalCompose remains compact with low communication and execution overhead. Proof. figure.figDesc: Figure1, CausalComposefirst extracts intervention-response evidence locally, validates the resulting causal dependencies, and then composes the validated structure with local mechanisms for downstream prediction and optional action guidance. This composition turns observational modular dynamics into an intervention-aware world model for planning. We theoretically show that causal recovery improves with intervention-response coverage and that, with sufficient coverage and controlled local mechanism error, causal composition can achieve lower intervention-time error than an observational world model.We evaluate these predictions through synthetic causal diagnostics and modular LLM-agent environments[3, 15,17,29,37]. The synthetic experiments verify the predicted intervention gap, horizon compounding, and dependence of causal recovery on intervention coverage. Agent experiments further show that incorporating causal structure improves intervention-sensitive reasoning and planning, with the clearest gains in structured tool-use environments[3, 15,17,37] where modular dependencies directly govern valid actions and downstream transitions. Across dialogue and narrative settings, the experiments further demonstrate that causal knowledge becomes useful when it is presented in a form that makes the relevant dependency actionable at decision time. Together, these results answer the question posed by our title: causal world models help modular LLM agents when intervention-sensitive dependencies can be identified from available evidence and incorporated into agent planning.Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We identify a fundamental mismatch between observational world modeling and intervention-time planning in modular LLM agents.
